\section{Per-Layer Gate Profile}\label{sec:appendix-gate-profile}

Table~\ref{tab:gate-profile} reports the final per-layer gate values for ThreadGate (seed 123) on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct (28 layers). Gate values are averaged across all tokens in the evaluation set. Layers 1 and 5 show the lowest gate values (0.793 and 0.797), indicating these layers are most amenable to attenuation without disrupting NTP. Layers 26--27 converge to $\geq$0.988, consistent with NTP gradient pressure dominating at output-adjacent layers. The mean across all layers is 0.947 ($\sigma$\,=\,0.051).

The gate profile exhibits two notable patterns: (1)~a bimodal dip at L1 and L5, suggesting two distinct ``dispensable'' layer clusters in Qwen's architecture; (2)~monotonic increase from L17 to L27, indicating output-adjacent layers are progressively more critical for NTP. Seed 42 produces a similar profile (mean 0.934, min at L3--L5), confirming the pattern is not seed-dependent.

\paragraph{Cross-model comparison.} Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (32 layers) shows a qualitatively different profile: a V-shaped valley at mid-to-late layers (L25\,=\,0.719, L24\,=\,0.809) rather than early-layer dips. Both architectures converge toward identity at output-adjacent layers, but the location of maximum attenuation differs---early for Qwen, late-middle for Llama---suggesting that layer importance hierarchies are architecture-dependent rather than universal.

\section{Scheduled Sampling Implementation}\label{sec:appendix-ss}

Our scheduled sampling implementation follows \citet{bengio2015scheduled} with modifications for multi-turn transformer training:

\paragraph{Sampling schedule.} The model-generated context ratio $\rho$ increases linearly from 0 to 0.5 over 3 epochs. At each training step, a Bernoulli trial with probability $\rho$ determines whether the input prefix is replaced with model-generated tokens. The effective usage rate (29.7--37.1\%) is lower than the nominal schedule due to per-sample Bernoulli variance.

\paragraph{Context generation.} When model-generated context is selected, the model autoregressively generates the assistant turns from the conversation prefix up to the current training position. The generated tokens replace the ground-truth assistant tokens in the input, while user turns remain unchanged. This preserves the multi-turn structure while introducing distributional diversity in the conditioning context.

\paragraph{Training dynamics.} The scheduled sampling variant converges to similar final loss (NTP 0.932 vs.\ 0.930 for standard ThreadGate) but with higher variance in early epochs due to the stochastic context mixing. Gate profiles remain similar (mean 0.953 vs.\ 0.947, min at L4 vs.\ L1), indicating that scheduled sampling does not fundamentally alter gate optimization but rather improves the robustness of the learned attention patterns to distributional shift. Training time increases approximately 60\% due to the autoregressive generation overhead during training (6.5h vs.\ 6.0h on Qwen; 10.8h for the seed-123 variant which uses a longer schedule).

\paragraph{Parameter overhead.} ThreadGate adds ${\sim}$57K gate parameters for Qwen-2.5-7B (28 layers $\times$ 2K per gate MLP) and ${\sim}$65K for Llama-3.1-8B (32 layers), representing $<$0.001\% of the base model. LoRA adapters (rank 16, targeting $q$/$v$ projections) contribute 4.2M parameters across both architectures.

\paragraph{Training time.} Standard variants (ThreadGate, Uniform Gate, LoRA-only) train in 6.0--7.3 hours. PCGrad adds ${\sim}$20\% overhead due to the per-step gradient projection computation. Scheduled sampling overhead varies: seed 42 adds only 8\% (6.5h) due to efficient batched generation, while seed 123 adds 80\% (10.8h) because of a longer generation schedule. The difference is due to the extended AR generation schedule in the seed 123 variant.

\paragraph{Inference overhead.} Gate computation at inference time is negligible: a single 32$\to$64$\to$1 MLP forward pass per layer adds $<$0.1\% latency. $\beta$-steering requires identifying goal tokens (a one-time operation per conversation) and adding a constant bias to attention logits, with zero additional parameters.

\section{Qualitative Steering Examples}\label{sec:appendix-examples}

Table~\ref{tab:examples} illustrates the effect of $\beta$-steering on model behavior in a 4-turn conversation where the system prompt instructs ``Always respond in exactly three bullet points.''

\begin{table*}[h]
\centering\small
\caption{Qualitative effect of $\beta$-steering on instruction following across conversation turns. System prompt: ``Always respond in exactly three bullet points.'' ThreadGate checkpoint, 4-turn conversation.}
\label{tab:examples}
\begin{tabular}{c p{5.5cm} p{5.5cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Turn} & \textbf{$\beta$\,=\,0 (unsteered)} & \textbf{$\beta$\,=\,3 (steered)} \\
\midrule
1 & \checkmark~Three bullet points, on-topic & \checkmark~Three bullet points, on-topic \\
2 & \checkmark~Three bullet points, relevant & \checkmark~Three bullet points, relevant \\
3 & $\sim$~Four bullet points, partially on-topic & \checkmark~Three bullet points, on-topic \\
4 & \texttimes~Free-form paragraph, no bullets & \checkmark~Three bullet points, on-topic \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table*}

The pattern is consistent with the GAR decay analysis: unsteered models progressively lose attention to the system-prompt constraint, leading to format violations at later turns. Steering maintains goal-token attention, preserving instruction compliance. Content constraints (e.g., ``never mention X'') show the largest improvement (+23.8\,pp at $\beta$\,=\,3; Table~\ref{tab:ir-results}), while format constraints that are more procedural show no change, consistent with the hypothesis that GAR captures attention to semantic goal content rather than procedural formatting rules.

This paper traces the failure to exposure bias \citep{bengio2015scheduled}: attention patterns optimized under teacher-forced prefixes do not transfer to model-generated text, even when next-token prediction (NTP) remains robust.
4	
5	Multi-turn attention decay is well-documented---\citet{dongre2026attention} showed that the Goal Accessibility Ratio (GAR), measuring attention to system-prompt goal tokens, declines 27--48\% across 12 models (we observe 70.8\% on Qwen-2.5-7B) while residual stream probes retain goal content (AUC\,=\,0.98)---but three research gaps remain open. No work examines how per-layer transformer behavior varies across conversation turns (the \emph{turn$\times$depth} gap). Existing remediations---split-softmax \citep{li2024measuring}, StreamingLLM \citep{xiao2024streaming}, gated attention \citep{qiu2025gated}---operate at inference time or are turn-agnostic; \emph{training-time} multi-turn attention optimization is unexplored. And classical exposure bias mitigation \citep{bengio2015scheduled,lamb2016professor} targets RNN sequence generation; no \emph{multi-turn transformer equivalent} exists.
6	
7	ThreadGate addresses these gaps with per-layer content-and-turn-conditioned MLP gates on the residual stream: $x_{l+1} = x_l + g_l \cdot f_l(x_l)$, where $g_l$ is a two-layer network conditioned on hidden states and turn position. A five-way controlled comparison---ThreadGate, +PCGrad, Uniform Gate, LoRA-only, Base---isolates turn conditioning, gating, gradient conflict, and fine-tuning (\S\ref{sec:comparison-design}), where each adjacent pair kills exactly one alternative hypothesis.

2	
3	Fine-tuned to allocate 50\% of its attention to system-prompt goals (GAR\,=\,0.50 under teacher forcing), Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct retains only GAR\,=\,0.064 under autoregressive generation---an 8$\times$ collapse that widens to 27$\times$ on Llama-3.1-8B.
